query_text: Why are some species so much more endangered than others?

messages.content: Why are some species so much more endangered than others?

message.content:
Some species are much more endangered than others because they face **stronger pressures from human activity and environmental change**, and because some species are inherently **less able to recover** from those pressures.[1][3][6]

The biggest drivers are **habitat loss and fragmentation**, **overexploitation** (hunting, fishing, harvesting), **pollution**, **invasive species**, **disease**, and **climate change**.[1][2][3][6] U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service says habitat loss is the main force behind today’s elevated extinction rate, with other threats such as over-exploitation, harmful nonnative species, pollution, and disease also playing major roles.[3] The University of Georgia article similarly notes that endangerment usually comes from multiple overlapping causes, often linked to human activities.[1]

Some species are hit harder because they have **small or isolated populations**, **specialized habitat needs**, or **low genetic diversity**.[1][5] Low genetic diversity reduces a species’ ability to cope with disease, weather extremes, and other stressors, making extinction more likely when conditions worsen.[1][5] Species that already live in limited ranges—such as island species, freshwater species, or animals tied to one habitat type—tend to be more vulnerable because losing even a small amount of habitat can have a large impact.[3][6]

A species’ risk also depends on how fast it can adapt or move. Species with **slow reproduction**, **narrow diets**, **restricted geographic ranges**, or **poor dispersal ability** usually recover more slowly after population declines, so the same threat can push one species toward extinction while another survives.[1][5][6]

In short, species become unevenly endangered because of a combination of **external pressures** and **biological vulnerability**: some face more intense human-caused threats, and some have fewer defenses against them.[1][3][5][6]
